blocks.text: I can understand the different uses of the possessive adjective ‘su’ in the context of learning about people and places in Mexico.
Lucía and Daniel are researching the people and the culture of Mexico for a family trip.
Tap each word to see what it means.

items.def: word that goes before a noun to show ownership or belonging

blocks.text: Mexico is famous for many things:
The capital is called la Ciudad de México, or ‘Mexico City’.
When ‘Tierra’ is used for the planet, use a capital letter.
These describing words change their ending for masculine and feminine, except one.
‘Muerto/a’ can also be used as a noun. The meaning would be ‘dead person’.

blocks.q: Match each Spanish word to its English meaning.

blocks.text: The verb **venir** means ‘to come, coming’. It is similar to **tener** (to have).
Like tener, venir has a stem change from e to ie in its ‘you’, ‘he, she’ and ‘they’ forms. The ‘I’ form vengo is irregular: we add {-g-}, like hago, pongo and salgo.

slides.title: His, her or its: su and sus

blocks.text: Possessive adjectives go before nouns to show belonging and ownership.

items: {su} = ‘his’, ‘her’ or ‘its’ before a singular noun: su país (his, her, its country)
{sus} = ‘his’, ‘her’ or ‘its’ before a plural noun: sus padres (his, her, its parents)
Su comunidad es especial. (His, her, its community is special.)
Sus costumbres son únicas. (His, her, its customs are unique.)

blocks.text: You can use {su(s)} with masculine and feminine nouns. Use **es** for a singular noun and **son** for a plural noun.

blocks.q: Choose su or sus to complete each sentence.

items.q: ___ playa es muy hermosa. (Its beach is very beautiful.)
___ ciudades son interesantes. (Its cities are interesting.)
___ abuelos son simpáticos. (Her grandparents are kind.)
___ perro es simpático. (His dog is kind.)

blocks.text: Su and sus agree with the noun that follows, and so does the verb. One thing: es. Many things: son.

blocks.q: Choose es or son to complete each sentence.

items.q: Sus playas ___ hermosas. (Its beaches are beautiful.)
Su ciudad ___ interesante. (Its city is interesting.)
Su canción ___ muy famosa. (Her song is very famous.)
Sus museos ___ geniales. (His museums are great.)

blocks.text: Su and sus have several meanings: his, her, its. To know which, we often need to use the context given in the surrounding text.

items: México es un país fascinante. Sus costumbres son únicas. (Mexico is a fascinating country. Its customs are unique.)
Carlos Santana es un guitarrista mexicano. Su talento es único. (Carlos Santana is a Mexican guitarist. His talent is unique.)

blocks.label: How do we know su means ‘his’ here?
blocks.text: The text is about Carlos Santana, and Carlos is a boy’s name. So su means ‘his’.

items.title: Chichén Itzá
items.sub: a cultural landmark. It was an important Mayan city, with a pyramid called ‘el castillo’.

blocks.q: What does su mean in each description?

items.q: Es una cantante mexicana. Su canción es muy famosa.
Es un actor mexicano. Su película ganó muchos premios.
Es una pirámide muy antigua. Su altura es de 30 metros.
Es un autor mexicano. Su libro habla sobre la comunidad mexicana.

blocks.q: Which sentence means ‘Its museums are great’?
blocks.why: Museums is plural, so we use sus and the verb son.

blocks.q: Which sentence means ‘Its people are very kind’? (Remember: ‘people’ in Spanish is singular.)
blocks.why: Gente is singular in Spanish, so we use su and es.

items: Mexico is famous for many things including its artists, its archaeology, its food, its customs and its unique history.
Possessive adjectives go before nouns to show belonging and ownership.
Su is ‘his’, ‘her’ or ‘its’ before a singular noun, e.g. su país. Sus is ‘his’, ‘her’ or ‘its’ before a plural noun, e.g. sus padres.
Su and sus have different meanings, so you will often need context to translate them accurately.

flashcards.front: Do “su” and “sus” change for masculine and feminine nouns?
flashcards.back: No. You can use su(s) with masculine and feminine nouns.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: People and places in Mexico: possessive adjective ‘su’
worksheet.instructions: Answer each question with a short answer. Some answers are in Spanish and some are in English. Use su and sus for ‘his’, ‘her’ or ‘its’.

questions.explanation: The ‘they’ form of venir is vienen (stem change e to ie).
The ‘I’ form of venir is irregular: vengo, with a -g-.
The feminine form of mexicano is mexicana.

questions.prompt: Write in Spanish: “custom” (one word, no el or la).
Complete with su or sus: ___ playas son hermosas. (Its beaches are beautiful.)
questions.explanation: Playas is plural, so we use sus.

questions.prompt: Complete with su or sus: ___ ciudad es interesante. (Its city is interesting.)
questions.explanation: Ciudad is singular, so we use su.

questions.prompt: Complete with es or son: Sus museos ___ geniales. (Its museums are great.)
questions.explanation: Museos is plural, so the verb is son.
Grandparents is plural, so we use sus.

questions.prompt: In “Es un autor mexicano. Su libro habla sobre la comunidad mexicana.”, does su mean his, her or its?
questions.explanation: The text is about an author (un autor), a man, so su means his.

questions.prompt: In “Es una pirámide muy antigua. Su altura es de 30 metros.”, does su mean his, her or its?
questions.explanation: A pyramid is a thing, so su means its.

questions.prompt: In “Es una cantante mexicana. Su canción es muy famosa.”, does su mean his, her or its?
questions.explanation: Una cantante is a woman, so su means her.
